chapter: Clarinet teachers and the Baton Rouge scene
title: Free clarinet lessons from Isadore Fritz
summary: Joe kept studying with Roque while Fritz, a Standard Oil worker, showed him things for free when he visited his father.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Picking up the first horn: clarinet and saxophone beginnings

blocks.x: Well, let us get along with how you learned to play "pretty good," as you say in your own word. Why did you quit going to, or did you quit going to Manuel Roque and go to Isadore Fritz? Or did one just drift into your life? How did that...?
I never did quit Manuel Roque. I learned more or less from both of them. But the only difference was I didn't have to pay Fritz.
Why didn't you have to pay him?

Well, Fritz never did ask for any money. He'd come right in, Papa would fix his shoes or something like that... And Fritz I don't think had any pupils. Fritz didn't teach. Fritz would just come there, and every time he came there, Papa... They had a place in Baton Rouge called the Standard Oil Company where all of these guys worked. That's where mostly everybody worked, was Standard Oil. That's the only big place that hired people. And they had to go by my houses to catch little flatbed train, flatcars called a Duberbug, and ride about ten miles, which was in Scotland. So when Fritz would come by the house, he was always talking to Papa; Papa was having a little nip or something... Prohibition was still in, but... Anyway, they'd get a beer or something; they had a saloon across the street, and they'd talk. And Papa would say, "Joe, go get
your clarinet and let Fritz show you something." And sure enough, Fritz would grab that clarinet and, man, his fingers... He was a much better clarinet player than Manuel.
